title: Exponents and Powers: Laws, Negative Exponents and Standard Form

sections.title: Powers with negative exponents
sections.body: You already know that a positive exponent tells you how many times to multiply a number by itself: 10³ = 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000. But what does a negative exponent mean? Look at the pattern as the exponent on 10 decreases by 1 each time: 10² = 100, 10¹ = 10, 10⁰ = 1 — each step divides the previous value by 10. Continuing that same pattern past zero, 10⁻¹ must be 1/10, 10⁻² must be 1/100, and so on. In general, for any non-zero integer a and positive integer m, a⁻ᵐ = 1/aᵐ. This also tells you that a⁻ᵐ and aᵐ are multiplicative inverses of each other, since aᵐ × a⁻ᵐ = a⁰ = 1. One subtlety worth watching: the sign of the final answer depends on aᵐ, not on the exponent being negative — (−2)⁻³ = 1/(−2)³ = 1/(−8) = −1/8 stays negative because the power itself is odd, while (−2)⁻² = 1/(−2)² = 1/4 turns positive because the power is even. This same idea extends how you write a decimal number in expanded form: just as 1425 = 1×10³ + 4×10² + 2×10¹ + 5×10⁰, a number like 1425.36 continues the pattern past the decimal point using negative powers of 10: 1425.36 = 1×10³ + 4×10² + 2×10¹ + 5×10⁰ + 3×10⁻¹ + 6×10⁻².

sections.title: Laws of exponents
sections.body: The exponent laws you learned for positive exponents keep working exactly the same way once negative and zero exponents are allowed. The product law says aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ — for example, 2⁻³ × 2⁻⁴ = 2⁻⁷, since −3 and −4 simply add together like any other integers. The quotient law says aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ, so 3⁷ ÷ 3⁻² = 3⁹, because subtracting a negative exponent is the same as adding its positive value. The power-of-a-power law says (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ — the two exponents multiply together — and this is especially useful for rewriting a power with an unfamiliar base as a power of a smaller, related base: since 16 = 2⁴, 16⁻¹ = (2⁴)⁻¹ = 2⁻⁴. When two different bases share the same exponent, they can be combined: aᵐ × bᵐ = (ab)ᵐ, and dividing works the same way, aᵐ/bᵐ = (a/b)ᵐ — this second law is what lets you evaluate a power of a fraction like (2/3)⁻² by flipping the fraction and making the exponent positive: (2/3)⁻² = (3/2)² = 9/4. Finally, any non-zero base raised to the power 0 equals 1 — even if that base is itself a complicated expression like (3⁻¹ + 4⁻¹ + 5⁻¹), as long as you can tell it isn't zero, its zeroth power is 1 without needing to evaluate the expression inside at all. These laws often need to be applied one after another in the same problem — simplify step by step, working with brackets and powers-of-powers first, the same order of operations you'd use anywhere else. Occasionally a problem runs the product law in reverse: if you're told two powers of the same base are equal, like (−4)ᵐ⁺¹ × (−4)³ = (−4)⁹, then the exponents themselves must be equal, giving a simple equation (m + 1 + 3 = 9) you can solve for the unknown.

sections.title: Standard form for very small numbers
sections.body: Very small measurements — the diameter of a red blood cell, the charge on an electron, the thickness of a sheet of paper — are awkward to write and compare as long strings of zeros. Standard form fixes this the same way it does for very large numbers, but with a negative exponent: any positive number can be written as k × 10ⁿ, where k is a number from 1 up to (but not including) 10, and n is an integer. For a small number, n is negative. To convert 0.000007 to standard form, count how many places the decimal point has to move to the right so that exactly one non-zero digit sits before it: it moves 6 places, giving 7 × 10⁻⁶. The same idea works for any small decimal — 0.0016 becomes 1.6 × 10⁻³, since the decimal point moves 3 places. Going the other way, from standard form back to an ordinary decimal, you move the decimal point left by exactly as many places as the (positive value of the) exponent: 7.54 × 10⁻⁴ becomes 0.000754, moving the point 4 places left and filling in zeros as needed.

sections.title: Comparing and combining very large and very small numbers
sections.body: Standard form makes it possible to compare wildly different sizes at a glance. To find out how many times bigger one quantity is than another, divide the two standard-form numbers: the diameter of the Sun (1.4 × 10⁹ m) divided by the diameter of the Earth (1.4 × 10⁷ m) gives 10⁹⁻⁷ = 10² = 100, so the Sun's diameter is about 100 times the Earth's. Adding or subtracting numbers in standard form takes one extra step first: the two numbers need to share the same power of 10 before their front parts (coefficients) can simply be added or subtracted. To add the mass of a planet, 3.2 × 10²³ kg, to its much lighter moon, 4 × 10²¹ kg, first rewrite 3.2 × 10²³ as 320 × 10²¹ so both numbers share the exponent 21 — then 320 × 10²¹ + 4 × 10²¹ = 324 × 10²¹, which renormalises back to standard form as 3.24 × 10²³ kg. Subtraction works the same way: rewrite both numbers with a matching power of 10 first, then subtract the coefficients directly.

workedExamples.problem: Find the value of 3⁻⁴ and the multiplicative inverse of 5⁻².
steps: The multiplicative inverse of 5⁻² is 5², since a⁻ᵐ and aᵐ are multiplicative inverses of each other.
workedExamples.finalAnswer: 3⁻⁴ = 1/81, and the multiplicative inverse of 5⁻² is 25.

workedExamples.problem: Express 9⁻³ as a power with base 3, then simplify (2³)⁻² × 2⁵ fully.
Express 0.0000523 in standard form, then convert 6.1 × 10⁻⁵ back to usual decimal form.
steps: For 0.0000523, move the decimal point right until exactly one non-zero digit remains before it: it moves 5 places, from 0.0000523 to 5.23.
For 6.1 × 10⁻⁵, move the decimal point 5 places left: 6.1 → 0.61 → 0.061 → 0.0061 → 0.00061 → 0.000061.

workedExamples.problem: A dust particle has a mass of about 7.5 × 10⁻¹⁰ kg and a grain of sand has a mass of about 7.5 × 10⁻⁷ kg. About how many times heavier is the grain of sand?
workedExamples.finalAnswer: The grain of sand is about 1000 times heavier than the dust particle.

objectives.text: Evaluate a power with a negative integer exponent by rewriting it as 1/aᵐ.
Find the multiplicative inverse of a power with a negative exponent.
Identify the exponent of 10 attached to a given digit in the expanded form of a decimal, including negative exponents for digits after the decimal point.
Apply the product law aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ for integer exponents, including negative ones.
Apply the quotient law aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ for integer exponents.
Apply the power-of-a-power law (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ, including re-expressing a power with one base as a power with a related base.
Apply aᵐ × bᵐ = (ab)ᵐ to combine two same-exponent powers with different bases.
Apply (a/b)ᵐ = aᵐ/bᵐ to evaluate powers of fractions, including negative exponents.
Apply a⁰ = 1 for any non-zero base expression.
Simplify expressions that combine two or more laws of exponents in sequence.
Find an unknown exponent in an equation of two equal-base powers.
Convert a very small decimal number to standard form (k × 10⁻ⁿ, 1 ≤ k < 10).
Convert a number given in standard form (negative exponent) back to its usual decimal form.
Compare two numbers given in standard form by computing the ratio of their magnitudes.
Add or subtract numbers given in standard form by first rewriting them with the same power of 10.
